title: Plan mode before replacing the homegrown authorization layer
situation: A payments platform team is replacing its homegrown authorization layer with a policy engine across API handlers, middleware, and tests. Engineers disagree about where the policy boundary should live, and the developer assigned to it is unfamiliar with several affected packages.
question: Which workflow should they choose before implementation?

options.A: Run a custom slash command that instructs Claude Code to avoid asking questions during the refactor.
options.B: Use direct execution so Claude Code starts editing immediately and discovers the architecture through test failures.
options.C: Enter plan mode so Claude Code researches the codebase and proposes changes for approval before editing files.
options.D: Select the opus model alias and let Claude Code complete the refactor through direct execution.

why: Plan mode is designed for work where it is valuable to separate investigation from implementation. In Claude Code, plan is a documented permission mode where Claude can research the codebase, may run exploratory shell commands subject to the normal permission flow, and writes a plan before source edits occur. The key operational boundary is that Claude Code does not edit source files until the plan is approved. Anthropic's best-practices guidance recommends planning when the user is uncertain about the approach, the change modifies multiple files, or the user is unfamiliar with the code being changed; all three conditions are present here, so direct execution is a poor fit even if it might be faster for small fixes. Selecting a stronger model can help Claude reason through difficult code, but model choice does not replace the workflow control and approval boundary provided by plan mode. (Docs: Claude Code permission modes, best practices, model configuration.)
concrete_task: claude -p "<refactor brief>" --permission-mode plan --allowedTools Read Grep Glob

tasks.prompt: We are replacing the homegrown authorization layer (src/middleware/authorize.js) with a policy engine across API handlers, middleware and tests. Engineers disagree where the policy boundary should live. Research the codebase and propose a plan with the boundary options for approval.

expected_outcome: Claude researches src/middleware/authorize.js and its callers and returns a plan; the file-hash table shows zero edits.

rubric.criterion: the output is a plan that names the authorization boundary
the plan references the real callers found by research
